meta_description: Mark Latimer set out to reach 3,000 solopreneurs with his ChatGPT courses. How to market a course with partners, free copies, referrals and video answers.
h1: How to market an online course
sub: Mark Latimer set out to reach 3,000 solopreneurs with his ChatGPT courses in a year, without a big team or a big ad budget. On this live coaching episode we worked out how: sell through partners, give copies away on purpose, ask for reviews and referrals, and answer questions on video.

video.title: Live Coaching: Marketing a Live Learning Cohort - Mark Latimer
video.description: Mike Moll coaches Mark Latimer of Art of ChatGPT on how to market an online course as a solopreneur: partner revenue shares, giving copies away, review and referral asks, outcome-led ads and video answers in online groups.

author.name: Mike Moll
author.byline_role: Sales + Offer Coach · with Mark Latimer
author.role: Sales + Offer Coach · Host of The Undervalued Expert
author.bio: After building 150+ offers, Mike has found that 90% of the problems service founders face are due to the offer. He has reviewed 1,000+ sales calls and has been a guest on 70+ podcasts.

guest.name: Mark Latimer
guest.bio: Mark teaches solopreneurs how to use ChatGPT in their business. His free course, iPhone Mastery for ChatGPT, is where he suggests most people start.

short_answer.q: How do you market an online course when you're a team of one?
short_answer.a: Sell through people who already have your audience. Find businesses that sell something next to your course and split the revenue with them, give free copies to people who run big communities, and ask every happy student for a review and a referral. Work out what one subscriber is worth to you first, so you know how much you can give away to get the next one.

takeaways: Make the course good first. Mark interviews beta users when they finish and uses what they say to improve it.
Sell through partners whose audience would love your course and who don't sell the same thing, for a revenue share.
A recorded course costs nothing to copy, so give it away on purpose to people who run communities.
Happy students rarely tell anyone. Ask for a review in an automated email when they finish.
Know what one subscriber is worth to you, then reward referrals with something that costs you less.
Don't overwhelm buyers with a thousand prompts or 85 hours of video. Sell an outcome a student had from the course.

sections.h2: Why does the course have to be good before you market it?
sections.html:
Mark runs Art of ChatGPT, where he teaches solopreneurs to use ChatGPT in their business. His free course, iPhone Mastery for ChatGPT, starts on your phone, so using it becomes a daily habit. When we recorded this, his goal was to serve 3,000 solopreneurs in a year.

When I asked how he planned to get there, he started with the product. The course has to be good enough that people finish it and tell someone. He's interviewing beta users when they finish, and he uses what they say to improve the course and to write content that turns visitors into active users.

I agree with that order. Every idea below works better when the people who take the course come out the other side with a win.

sections.h2: How do you sell a course through someone else's audience?
sections.html:
Find people who sell something next to your course and let them sell it for you. I'm doing this with my course on how to get booked on podcasts. One company I talk to helps people become authors. They help write, publish and market the book, and one of their services is booking authors on podcasts. Some of their clients will never pay for that service, so I asked them to sell my course to those clients at whatever price they like and keep a percentage. A few PR firms are doing the same.

The test is simple: their audience would love what you do, and you aren't competing for the same dollars.

For Mark, that means marketing agencies and training companies with a lot of small-business clients. They can sell his ChatGPT courses as part of their own programs on something like a 50/50 revenue share. Once it's set up, it's a channel he doesn't have to work.

The same idea, for servicesGetting booked as a podcast guest works the same way. The host already has the audience, and they hear you on a show they trust. The podcast guesting workshop covers how to do it.

sections.h2: Why give a digital course away for free?
sections.html:
Once a course is recorded, another copy costs you nothing. That changes what you can afford to give away.

My podcast course sells for $375, and it paid for itself in the first four sales. So when someone I want on board asks what it costs, I send them a copy. They get a $375 course, and it costs me nothing to send.

Mark can do the same with bigger groups. Donate ten copies as prizes at a conference or an association event. Give five copies to someone who runs a large community, for their best members, and ask for feedback. If they like it, set up an affiliate deal. You earn trust with that community before you ask it for anything.

sections.h2: Why won't a good course sell itself?
sections.html:
Mark said a course that's done well should market itself, and a good course does a lot of the work. The catch is that happy customers stay quiet. When someone loves a course, they keep it to themselves and mention it only if a friend asks. When someone hates a course, they post about it.

So build the ask into the course. Set up an automated email that goes out when someone reaches the end. Ask for a review or a testimonial, and tell them why it matters: it helps you reach more people like them. Asking in plain, grateful words has gotten me good responses.

The course has to respect people's time too. I once paid for a personal branding course from a big name that was a string of YouTube videos with no direction. Mark has spent a lot of time editing his so people want to keep going, and that's the kind of course people finish and recommend.

sections.h2: How do referral rewards work for a course?
sections.html:
Give people a reason to share, and make sharing one click. Here's what I do with my newsletter. Every subscriber gets a link to share. If 20 people sign up through it, they get a free half hour with me to solve a big problem in their business. I've charged up to $1,000 for one hour.

Mark can do the same with what he already has. Get 20 people into the course and you get the other courses free, or a spot in a program. If the first course helped someone, they'll share it when sharing is easy.

I can give that away because I know what a subscriber is worth to me. When we recorded this, every 25 people on my list brought in about $275 on average, through courses or one-off consulting. Once you know that figure, you can compare a referral reward with what ads would cost you. Referrals come with proof built in, too. A friend posting "I took this and it was great" converts better than any post you write about yourself.

sections.h2: What should a course ad say?
sections.html:
Mark asked how I'd advertise his course on Instagram or Facebook. I'd lead with one outcome a student got. Most AI course ads offer a thousand prompts for $27, or a course with 85 hours of material. As a solopreneur, I don't want more to get through. I want the answer.

Take three stories from your exit interviews: the hours a student saved each week, or the agency they stopped paying because they could do the job themselves. People see themselves in other people's outcomes and think, "I want that." The ad is the teaser that gets that reaction. The landing page gives the details of what they get.

sections.h2: How do you get seen without paying for ads?
sections.html:
Answer people's questions on video where they're already asking them. Go through Reddit threads and Facebook groups and find people who are stuck. Record a short Loom of you solving their problem in ChatGPT, step by step. Loom lets you add a call to action to the video, so it can point to your course. If you spend seven minutes solving someone's problem, it's fair to mention your course at the end.

I do a version of this every week. I used to write long answers to people's questions. Now I answer 8 to 10 a week on Loom. Each one is YouTube content, it gives me clips for other channels, and I run the transcript through a GPT I built for my brand voice to draft a blog post.

Mark added a recording tip from his side: record the full screen every time. You can crop later, but you can't go back and get the part you didn't record.

sections.h2: How long before posting consistently pays off?
sections.html:
For me it took about 60 days. I posted on LinkedIn three to four times a week and shared Instagram stories fairly regularly. Then I landed two contracts, possibly a third, worth about $45K, in 10 days. One of those leads told me they'd been keeping an eye on my content and had seen one of my ads.

Repetition is what makes people remember what you do. People start to think "Mike's the guy who does that thing." For Mark, the goal is that people think "Mark's the guy who makes AI easy."

At our stage, with no full team and nobody else as the face of the brand, that means making a lot of content for a while. Mark is planning for it with production blocks in his calendar, an assistant who finds questions on Reddit for him to answer, and editing he'll hand off once his course on editing with ChatGPT is recorded.

sections.h2: What can you do this week?
sections.html:
1. Write down three businesses that sell something next to your course, and ask each one to sell it for a revenue share.
  2. Pick five people who run communities your buyers are in, and send each of them a few free copies for their best members.
  3. Add an email that goes out when someone finishes the course and asks for a review in plain, grateful words.
  4. Work out what one subscriber is worth to you, then set a referral reward that costs you less than that.
  5. Answer one question a day on video in a group where your buyers spend time, and point to the course at the end.

If Facebook is where your buyers are, this episode with Megan Van Noy covers how to sell in groups without spamming them.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike

paragraphs.text: So ultimately, I want to serve a lot of people this year. Our goal is to serve 3,000 solopreneurs in some capacity. paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, absolutely. paragraphs.text: But when I'm faced with just a blank page, it's such an overwhelming feeling for me, and I, truthfully, I'm a procrastinator. I shut down. I buy a thing and I'm like, "Oh, that was really great, I loved it," and I put it in my back pocket, and if I'm talking to someone who's like, "Oh, how'd you learn this?"

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: "Oh, I took this great course." But most people don't go out of their way to do it. It's not natural. Whereas, you know, you go to a restaurant and you have a terrible experience, you buy some program, the next time you see the guy's Facebook post you're like, "Man, this was such a dumpster fire. What a waste of time. Nine hours to teach me what could have been done in 20 minutes."

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so one thing is, like, yes, it can sell itself, but how do we give that a little bit of push? How do we give that a little bit of, like, thrust in the right direction, especially as we're scaling? So a couple things that come to mind, some ideas that I'm playing with for myself, is making sure there's an automation post-purchase for, like, "Hey, they got to the end, hey, you know, are—" and it's like, in that, I like the idea of the grateful kind of terminology.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: "Hey, listen, we want to get this out and help as many people as possible. We'd be incredibly grateful if you could write a review or do a testimonial or whatever the case may be." So, like, getting that social proof on the back end, you know, kind of a standard idea, but, like, approaching it from a, like, "this is going to help us help more people, we'd really appreciate this," I found has gotten me, like, really good responses on it.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then, to compound that, and I think even more effectively, what I've been playing with is, like, not affiliate necessarily, but I don't even know what it would techn—I guess it's called affiliate, but without being, like, a monetary reward. But what I'm thinking about, like, for my email list, I put in this little thing that's like, "Hey, here's your link to share this. If you get 20 people to sign up to this email list, I will give you a free half an hour of my time. We'll go deep, we will, like, solve a big problem in your business."

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And normally I would charge, like, for an hour, you know, I've charged up to $1,000 basically for one hour. Now, I do a lot of work that goes in ahead of that to make sure, like, that hour is, like, a killer hour.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But, like, you know, what is that mechanism for you where it's like, "Hey, get, you know, get 20 people to sign up for this course and you will have, you know, all the courses for free," or "you get this program for free," or, you know, like, give them the benefit of more products or more things within your ecosystem.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Because if they really liked it, and that one thing helped, it's likelier if you make it easy, if you make it a one-click event. You know, "Hey, I'll put it on my email list. If I get 20 people to sign up, I get a bunch of stuff for free from Mark," which is going to help me, and then it just, that helps get that, helps get the thing out there. So I really like that idea.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: It's like, I'm using it for my newsletter right now, which is like just one click, just share this link on your social, share this link in your emails, whatever. If you can get some people on my list—like, because I know that, you know, for every 25 people on my list, I'm going to make, let's call it, an average of $275 bucks, whether that's a course, whether that's a one-off consulting, doesn't matter.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: But, like, so for every 25 people I'm going to make money, and once you have that measurement, once you know how much a subscriber or a free course person is worth in the big picture—sometimes it takes, you know, time to figure that out—but once you know, then it becomes, "Oh, okay, well, I could run, you know, I could run Facebook ads, or I could just give away that monetary thing, which is free for me anyway because the course is already there."

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so, like, leveraging that, and knowing I'm going to give away, you know, $300 worth of stuff for every 20 people that you bring to me, the power of that is really great, because it's social-proofed marketing, which is great. You know, it's not you posting saying, "This guy said it was good." It's that guy posting saying, "I took this thing, it was great, you should check it out." I mean, that is going to convert at a really good rate for you.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: Yeah, so much to think about there. There's no shortage of different things that you can apply. I'm curious, if you were to advertise this on, say, Instagram or Facebook, how would you approach it?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: That's a funny question and a great question. So my Sunday newsletter—this is unrelated, I know, we know each other—my Sunday newsletter is a screenshot of a bunch of promotions. If you're listening, I apologize. A bunch of promotions for chat prompts. And I've been taking screenshots of all the dumbest ChatGPT prompt promotions on the internet, and I'm going to write a post on Sunday, like, how to not sell AI training.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And again, it wasn't inspired by you, it was completely separate. It's because I see them all the time, and every ad is like, "Hey, here's a thousand prompts, and it's going to cost you $27." And it's like, I don't want a thousand prompts. You're not speaking to me. As a solopreneur, I don't need a thousand more things to do. I don't need 70 hours of course material.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: I was trying to learn something about ads the other day. I just wanted to do a bit of a refresher. I haven't run a campaign, I've strategized on them, but I'm not in it anymore as much, right? And this course was like, "Yeah, there's like 85 hours of material." I'm like, who wants to—I want one hour. Like, teach me the thing in one hour, let's get it done. And so here's what: give me 10 prompts that are the must-haves.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so when I think about whether it's organic posting or whether it's a paid ad, I think about, like, as a solopreneur, what would inspire me to buy it? It's not a volume game. It's not a quantity thing, because that makes me feel overwhelmed. That makes me feel like I'm never going to get through it. I'm going to open this book and I'm going to be like, I'm not going to read 3,000 pages on this thing. I just want the answer.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And so it's like, you know what I would do is, you've got these exit interviews where people are like, "Hey, this helped me learn this, this helped me gather this." I would tell a story. You know, "This course helped Mike cut down 15 hours of manual labor and content creation every single week."

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: "This course taught this person how to accomplish this thing without needing to go and hire, you know, multiple different vendors or multiple different agencies to do the thing." It's like, oh, that's what it does. Like, what is my outcome, and how, you know, did it do it quickly, did it do it efficiently, and what did it do for that person? I would just give three examples, because often we're going to see that in ourselves when we're reading it.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: We're like, "Oh yeah, I hate, like, I hate having to go to an agency for this thing, it drives me crazy. Like, if I could do it and it took me very little time, that would be such a godsend. I could train someone on my team to do it, and we would move on." And so they see themselves in what the outcome was for other people, and they're like, "I want that outcome for me, let me go check it out."

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Because the ad should be that teaser, that, like, let's—like, what's something where I connect with it and I'm like, "Oh, damn, if I had that, that'd be awesome." And then the landing page should expand on it and give us more—like, "Okay, what's, like, what are the actual details, what am I getting out of this thing?" But I think if you're going to do content and posts, which leads me to what I was thinking about when we were talking pre-call, which is, like, what do you do online to build your visibility, build the brand, build the whatever?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: I think what you do is you go through Reddit and Facebook groups and find people who are like, "I'm stuck on this thing," you know, "I'm thinking about hiring somebody," or "How do I deal with this?" or "What do I do?" I would just record Loom videos of you building, like, something in ChatGPT, like, "Hey, if I were you, I would do this," and just give a step-by-step instruction on it.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then when you save that video in Loom, you can create a call to action, so when you go to edit, you can make a call to action that's like, you know, "Get all the solopreneur AI secrets in this course." And you could drive traffic from that, because if you record a seven-minute video solving someone's problem, I think that's a fair thing to add a CTA on there saying, "Hey, come take this course." I do that all the time, so that would be a good way.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: And then if it gets viral and it gets views, you can kind of see how many people have seen it. It allows you to drive traffic, and then it's just a good function. Like, you're great at making content, and you've made the content that goes in the course, but I think, you know, almost kind of remaking pieces of it to answer people's questions, or "Hey, I've got a module, I'm just going to share the module," and drive the people through that. But I think that would be a really cool way for visibility and potential virality of some of the posts.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: I think ultimately I'm going to have to make a lot more content before I'm going to have to make a lot less content. So it's more important, I think, the habits. You know, do I have my blocks of time where it's just production? Where, you know, the daily rhythm of whether it's, to your point, going through, having my assistant sort some things on Reddit to kind of set me up for those recordings, but making those bursts and recordings optimal. And right now I'm doing a lot of the editing, because I'm also recording a course on how to use ChatGPT for editing, so there's some hands-on learning, and I can also narrate this stuff.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: If I wasn't doing the course, I wouldn't be doing the editing, so it's serving two purposes. But at some point I'll be handing that off, but now the training material will be all done for the editor. So it's been an interesting process. I've tried to get in the habit of doing a lot more screen recording, and now with tools like Descript, the AI video editor, there's a really great workflow, probably no different than Loom, that you have a ton of space, so you're not missing out on anything.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: And I was for a while only recording a section of the screen, but there's no point not to do full screen all the time, and then you can just clip whatever you want out of it. But you can't go back and get that part you didn't record, so just a lesson learned.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, yeah. That's honestly, that's been such a game changer for me.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Because I was writing long-form answers to questions for people, and then I'm like, this is stupid, I'm just going to respond to everything via Loom. So I've made it a habit of, like, if I respond to 8 to 10 things on Loom every single week, first of all, that's YouTube content. Second of all, there might be pieces or clips that get used elsewhere. Third of all, I take the transcripts into a GPT that I built for, like, my brand voice, and I'm like, "Write me a blog post based on the content of this." And so, like, I'm going so heavy on video first, and you're very good at it. Like, we're both good at producing videos.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: So yeah, that could be interesting, because then you're answering people in long, thoughtful ways where people are like, "Oh, damn, that's really helpful," you know, driving actual traffic to the site, and then repurposing it for everything else.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: I know the repurposing thing is tough. Like, I wish I just had someone full-time who's taking everything that I did and cutting it up.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: It is a pain. But I will say, you know, every time I do a run of content—I've been very consistent for the last 60 days, three to four times on LinkedIn a week, posting Instagram stories fairly regularly—like, I just landed three, well, landed two, possibly a third contract now. So we're talking about, like, $45K generated in 10 days, just because I'm—I know it's because when I'm out there, people see it. People, you know, that was one of the leads. They're like, "Yeah, I've been keeping an eye on your content, I think I saw one of your ads."

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: Oh, there you go. Perfect.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Like, that's what it is. It's that repeat, repeat, repeat. Mike's that guy. Mike's the guy that does that thing. Mark's the guy that makes AI easy for us, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: And where's the hat?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Exactly. And so, you know, I think there's a lot of value in that, and it is that trap of, like, I'm just constantly producing, producing, producing. But I think at the stage that we're at, where we don't have the full team, we don't have someone else that's the face of our brands, it's kind of just like, you know, suck it up for the next little bit, figure it out.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: Well, if you can have fun doing it, right? Like, we're on a journey, you know. You've been traveling for a little while, and waking up in a new place and creating some content feels great, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, absolutely. Perfect. Well, we ran a little bit over, so was anything else that you wanted to add in as we—

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: No, this has been a ton of fun. I appreciate you and your time.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Yeah, we'll have to get another episode going where we do some live AI training for my community.

paragraphs.speaker: Mark
paragraphs.text: Yeah, I'm happy to. To add one thing, it's an accessibility feature. So on your Mac, you can go to dictation, turn on sound, and you can change it to—now I have Control, Control: hit it twice and it turns on dictation. So right into ChatGPT from my laptop, I can do long thoughts and have it turn into prompts. That's a huge, huge time saver right there.

paragraphs.speaker: Mike
paragraphs.text: Cool. Well, go change that if you don't have it set already. I love it, man. Well, thanks so much, appreciate the time, brother, and I wish you all the best with the project.
